segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We’re gonna talk in Cherokee for a little while. We’re gonna talk for...

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: They talk differently now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The way we’re talking now sounds differently than what they did a long time ago.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: This is the second time he’s here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know what you think. In 20 years, if we’re still living, do you think this Cherokee language will still be going?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: For us that are still here, if we try real hard, it will still be going in the future. But if it stops, it’ll end. That’s what the old folks said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays the Indians are marrying the white people and their wives and husbands just like this One [points at Dianna].

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Just two of them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just like you’re saying, that what’s going to happen.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The Cherokees are also marrying the Mexicans nowadays.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some of the Mexicans are learning Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The white people are learning, too.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Some of them probably know more. The teachers here call me a lot. They’ll ask, “How do you say this? “Boy y’all are getting paid a lot over there and I’m not getting paid at all.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Y’all just want me to teach?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s what I was telling them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You oughta be the one that comes here. What’s your name in English and what’s your name in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Richard Lee Ross, Siqwanid, however they wanna say it. Siqwanid Wilam, Siqwanid Liw, they say.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that Ross?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: No, that was Ross, my older brother. His name was Gawisgage. My dad, Levi, some would say Gawisgage, which means Ross. My uncle's name was Wilam Gawisgage, United States Deputy Marshal.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I believed his name was Levi. That’s the guy I was telling you about that had the patch on his eye [talking to Guy] That was his dad you was talking about that one time.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That one that had a patch.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The one with the patch.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I’m about the last one there, by myself, that grew up there. I’m still in the same house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you’re still there.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: It’s still way better than the new ones they’ve built recently.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who lives in those houses close by?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Where George lived? Nobody. They was trying to sell it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember when they were trying to sell it.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Where I grew up, I lived by myself and below me Birdie lived there by himself. Where Ella used to live, Jerry. Above me, Red.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just you all guys there, huh?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Red’s wife and Jerry’s wife are the only women.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s right, they are married, huh. Jerry Ross, he comes here sometimes.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s my nephew.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s his nephew. [to Guy]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess it’s really changed, huh, or is it the same?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: The only difference is that some people have passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And now the kids moved in.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And now even they ain’t here, except Red’s grandkids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A lot has changed.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s what I say to them when they talk. They say, “That’s not how you say it.” We say things a lot different than they do. It’s almost like when we teach a child to ride a bicycle. Then when you push them, what would you say? “Do this.” “You would say “pedal - take a step”. But that’s not what you’re saying, you’re saying take a step”.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s right, huh?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Because it’s vodvnigawetli, they say back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Vodvnigawetli. That’s what they used to say. Then they would say, “Let’s dinigawetluga.” ‘Cause now you’re not saying taking step, now you’re saying pedal. That’s what they say to me when they come to me and I’m the last one born. But I’ve also experienced a lot. I’ve been taught things.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’ve never heard of that.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s the way it is if you’re not a real Cherokee. They weren’t getting on to you, they were teaching you. That’s what I’m thankful for, that people know enough to say, “Let’s ask Richard.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, they really all come to you. When you were a boy growing up. Were you making your own toys back then when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I was dealing with rocks and woods. There wasn’t really anything. If you found a board that was cut – it was just things like that. Or there was a junk pile going towards Ice Killer’s. That’s where we would be sticking out there, early Saturday morning. And way after a while people would come off the hill and throw stuff away. And after they left, we would get bicycle wheels and make bicycles to ride and we pedal on.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You guys had a lot of fun.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, Saturday was big day. I knew we would be dragging something back we never seen before.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did Ice throw stuff away?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: No, but Ice probably being stingy. Yeah, that’s just the way I grew up. I don’t even hardly [unclear]. You know the things they call posts made from locust? I was about seven years old. Over there, close to your house [Dianna], my brothers used to cut those, and I used to watch them. They were dragging some big ones by, and I was just little. I went and grabbed and picked one up and drug it and my dad was really looking at me. I said, “Look Dad!” and he said, “Now you found something to do.” Since then I started.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They put you to work.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s right, if you can do it, that’s your job.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can just see your dad saying that.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Boy, he won’t tell you the second time – he’ll get mad (usqwanoyvgo). Like we said, early they weren’t getting on to us. They were just telling us. It was really like that. I’ve been thinking about that for the last few days. When we thought we were really getting in trouble, they were just teaching us how to work so we could help ourselves.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And another thing, we weren’t crybabies. They wouldn’t feel sorry for us. They would just say, “Get up there’s nothing wrong with you.” That’s how we grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were really teaching us good.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, if we paid attention.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what you were saying, when they would tell us not to do something that is bad, they’re just teaching us not to do that.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And what they were teaching us is still going on. I really like to talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m really glad.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I’ve helped a lot of people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just talk about how you’ve helped people. What all have you done for them?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I’ve done a lot of things, and this One [Dianna] I saved from drowning. Do you remember that? We were swimming by George's house where there was a creek. And we were looking for you and saying, “Where did she go?” And it was flooding. I looked and all I could see was your hair floating in the water. I dove in and pulled you out by the hair and drug you back out.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, there was a little bridge there on this side where we were swimming, and you were going downstream, already drowning.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There’s no telling what I would do.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I don’t care what people say or think about me, and if they want something, I will still help them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was glad you helped me.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: We were all swimming there, Moon, Jen, Ollie, and Lilly.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was the good old time, but when it flooded, it was rough. And Bull, my uncle, had a horse, and we would ride it through that. And now I think about it, that was really dangerous. Sometimes the water was high, sometimes all you could see was the horse's head sticking out. The water was up this high, and I would just hold on to him while we crossed.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, me and Bull always riding that horse.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I wouldn’t do that now.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: There was a road on this side and where the bridge was where there’s water, and they called it the rock. And we would come out there. Around the curve is where the road is where y’all grew up, that’s where we would come out.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And that’s a long ways, right?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Everything was good a long time ago. As long as you didn’t have to work.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was a good place to swim. And we looked for crawdads there.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And me, I wished I had a better attitude a long time ago than the way it is now. I didn’t realize until I was almost 70 years old. The things I’ve done were dangerous. And going into big prisons. But I have learned that’s what my dad said. I wasn’t supposed to have made it on earth. I was two years old before I got home from the time I was born. And then a lot of medicine men were coming. I remember the last one that doctored me, I think his name was Eli Stick. Eli was the old man's name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where was he from?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Jay.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Jay, oh yeah.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Eliya I still have the picture. I’m just little. Standing up I’m like this [gestures] and here’s Eli and my dad. I’m standing below. My dad told me that this is what he said, “He’s going to get better but he’s going to see a lot of things, but there’s nothing going to happen to him.” They have given up on me. There were specialists. Two from Tulsa and one from Tahlequah that have given up on me. “You’re not gonna be able to get up, you’re not even going to be able to sit on the bed. Just a few more months and there’s no use in us talking about it.” I told them in English, “Y’all have a good day, I serve a higher power than you.” And I’m still here. It’s been four years since they gave up on me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, I have seen Eli Stick. I’ve seen him around.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: He was really a good healer and he was the one who healed. That’s why I’m still here.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was he coming from there and staying with you all?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, they would stay for two weeks, and there would probably be seven of them. My uncle John and dad and Eli and all of them doctored me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There’s not anyone left who does that now, medicine men.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: No, there are some but not that many, and most of them are just into the bad stuff. Some of them really like money. That’s what they told me and if they tell you they’re gonna charge you this [gestures] much, just turn around and leave and it’s not supposed to cost us anything. It’s just been given to us. Be thankful someone gives you something and don’t be charging for it, I was told.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what they used to say a long time ago.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Didn’t your dad know how to do that?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, he did know how to do that. Yeah. They all knew how to, like John and their sisters. That old lady that raised George Bunch was my aunt.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What was her name?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I’ll say it in a little bit.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did she live in Greasy?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, she lived by Billy Gonzalis, the first house.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can just see her, but I forgot what her name was.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: She wore a bandana. Her name was Ada in English. Ada Bunch.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s who raised George?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That was my aunt. She was my dad's sister. And also Viola’s mother. She’s my aunt, too, and also my dad's sister. And also Nel and Charley. Tlaneni – that’s Charley’s name in Cherokee. Their mother is also a sister to my dad.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I didn’t know that. I didn’t know all of them.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Really? We would hear what they’re saying but if we didn’t hear what they’re saying we wouldn’t know what it was. That’s what’s happening now. The people we know now, we would say, “Who is that? I can talk all night long.” That’s what they do at the house. They come out to visit me. Just the youngsters, they’ll just be sitting there, listening while I’m talking about stuff. I tell them that I’m not lying about the stuff I’m telling. I’ve seen it, been through it, and done it. "There would be no use in me lying to you all, because I don’t even know you all.” Why would I be lying to them?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, I think you did go through a rough time. Do the people that live by you come and see you or do they not come over?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Nope. I really want to visit your dad. We might work something out. Does he still have those trucks, the pickups? Does he? It’s been two years since I’ve broke down and no one tries to help me fix it. I used to fix them myself when I was a mechanic. I went to college but then my body became crippled.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Now it’s the Chevy, the one he was always driving around.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: The new one or the old one?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The older one. The new one was stolen.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The Pettits.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: The boys? Well, I looked into it for them. When that happened to him in Marble City, when they killed him. I was the one reading it and I told them, James Nofire, I was the one reading that and I told them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess they know what happened. We never heard anything else.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s what I was telling them and you all are saying all this stuff and in a few days it’ll be forgotten. That’s what I told them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess he just left in the middle of the night, they said.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: When he came out, he went around the house and went down the hill.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They found him somewhere by the water.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: They looked for him for three days and then I showed up. I told them, “Let’s go this way” and they said, “We’ll go over there after we eat.” In just 15 minutes after I showed up, they went over there and found him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What had happened to him? They didn’t know?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: No, they really didn’t know but think it was his heart. There was a bunch of stuff going on.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Didn’t they find him in the water?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: His shoes and socks were all tore up. It was like…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was dragged.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Like as if he was dragged through the stickers. And still nothing. I was telling them, “Y’all are just going to forget,” and they said no. And already it’s nothing.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And also, my dad said James would come to the house with no shoes. Even at night he would come up with no shoes on.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, he was like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: James Nofire, huh?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Have you ever heard of him?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: The people from Oak Ridge, Jerry the preacher was his. I don’t know his grandson?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I believe it was his grandson.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: It’s nothing now, but I don’t remember… Oh Maxy and his brother Gary Nofire, that was their dad, James.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, where I’m from, Jay, he stayed out there awhile. His name was James Nofire, too.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, there is also some that live there and also Kenwood. And that’s where they started from.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was just a boy. If he was still alive, he would probably be about 43.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, he was just about that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Right now, he would be that old. How long ago did he pass?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Been about five. Four or five years.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, he was just a young man.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The James Nofire, I was saying, who lived there, was about my age. He got him a woman whose name was Watermelon. And now the kids they have raised are still living. They sing around. They sing at churches and the young man’s name is Junior. And he has a white wife. They’re really good singers and they also sing at funerals. I guess they’re related.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way the family went a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you’re saying, when the boy would talk about it, he would say, “That’s where they live, my relatives.”

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Like what we’re talking about, this is what they done. People are amazed at what I have done. And I’ve done everything. Like you said, I’m a singer and I play music and like he said, I was going to see a lot of things, but nothing was going to happen to me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You was also fixing houses?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I was a builder. I was a builder for 35 years. And now it’s been a few years ago when I hurt my back and when that started, I had to shut down my own company and go on disability.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I really knew the guy Junior, he went to church at Belfont. It wasn’t long and he passed and – Nvwotvn I forgot his name – he went to church where Charlie Shell pastors. That one, Nvwotvn.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: James and Charlie Shell were related, huh. They were close.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, close. OK look here, Charlie's mom and my dad is siblings and also the Nofires, Columbus and the Pritchetts and you, George Pritchett, are all family.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Guess I learned something.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: It’s supposed to be like that a long time ago. A group of Cherokees, Creeks, or Choctaws wouldn’t marry anybody who was outside of the tribe. It had to be a Cherokee, not a Creek to call on. All Cherokee–Cherokee–Cherokee. That’s why we’re like this.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: A long time ago they didn’t like a Cherokee to be with a white. I asked my dad how that was when my granny married a white man. I wonder how the people felt about it back then.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And it wasn’t good and wasn’t easy for them to not show it, but they didn’t feel good about it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My dad’s mom was Cherokee, but his dad was white. Wonder what… at that time it wasn’t a good thing.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s what the white people were thinking, too, when we were in school. They didn’t like us Cherokees. And now if you go to the Indian hospital, you’ll see a white person.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: They told us it would be like that if we don’t pay attention.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they get mad at you when you married a White, a man?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No, it wasn’t like that back then.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: She’s young.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Back when my granny was young, they didn’t like it back then. A white getting a Cherokee and Cherokee getting with a white. They really didn’t like it and I don’t know why. Granny has been married twice. A white man…

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And also George.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And George was also half white.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And also, I think he got that from his mom’s side.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So, she was white.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, she was. And also, Dad’s brothers were all Cherokee. They were almost full blood. And now that’s what I am from that point forward. Let’s all sit around all day and talk about things and I really liked that and that’s why I know all the old stuff. And I also know where you came from. If someone just tells me one time, then later on, I’ll tell them how it is.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Moon and Jen look like white women. Larry’s sisters looked like white women – they had green eyes. Bull didn’t look like a white person, Gwen didn’t either. Just the girls looked like white people.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: They favored on that man's side.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ross’s eyes were like that, too. He got that from the Mexican side.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I don’t know what he got that from.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He favored his dad’s side, which was my grandpa. They’re Mexican.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: The whole time I was growing up, I thought Ross was my brother. That’s how we had it. That’s why he lives where he lives, on our property of 20 acres. My aunt, whose name was Udayi, was Ross’s mom. She was my dad's sister and when she died, my mom and dad didn’t have a child yet and so they took him in.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then they raised him.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: They raised him. And we were the ones getting whipped.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were teaching you good, weren’t they?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s why Angel’s name is Udayi.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Udayi put a saddle on when she was a little girl. I still got it. It doesn’t even have any leather on it, it’s just wood. It’s an old saddle. I have it hanging. It belongs to my aunt.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You said wahatv earlier, what is that?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What he said earlier, I don’t know. What did you say that meant?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You said something like... what.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Saddle – what’s that Cherokee?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Oh saddle? Gayvhulo.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gayvhulo.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Gayvhulo.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You said something else. Wahatv. Saddle is gayvhulo.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Gayvhulo. That’s why they say wiyayvhutlvgi. Go saddle it up!

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What I want in my own mind is to turn this back like they do on a TV. That’s what I wanna do.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: When you record it, you back up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what I wanna do in my own mind. Yeah, that’s what he said, watvhula. He did say something different. We’ll talk about it in a little bit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me and you should have had a recorder.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We can listen to it here.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I think I said awayvhutlvnvd. And what that is... Is she the one who used the saddle? Awayvhutlvnv and if you said wiyayvhutlvgi that means go do it. Awayvhutlvnv, that’s his or her saddle. It’s the same. If you make that different, you’ll say it different.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s right.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: They wanted me to write a book, and they said they already had it lined up for me. Jeffery Limore from Wichita, he said, “If you can write one page of the stories, you tell. He’ll write your book and everything is already lined up.” But I told them no. They told me, You’ll have your own book.” I don’t care. “You’ll make money.” That’s not what it’s for.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Jeff passed away, didn’t he?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I was always with white people. People were amazed I could speak good English. It’s not that I’m not able to speak English, it’s because I don’t know who you’re acting like, and I don’t wanna be all the way up here and for you to be way down here. I wanna look at you, eye to eye. And that’s why I translated a lot in Muskogee Federal Court. I’ll interpret for Indian people. I’m not just [unclear] here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You’re translating. They would tell you to keep translating.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I couldn’t figure it out when they called me on the phone, saying they picked me for the 29th. They only picked a few of them and you’re one of them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Also, how many kids were all of you? How many kids were all of you?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I had 10. But where we’re from, one time there was 56 of us looking for a [unclear]. All of the 57 family members a long time ago everywhere.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You all lived close together.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: On our land Ross Mount.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all were really close back then.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, used to be.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, all lived really close.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: There are about 15 houses with everybody, the Rosses. One way in and one way out. People used to be afraid to come over there. “I don’t wanna go up there, not with the Rosses.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They thought they would go in there for good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, you’d go in there forever if you didn’t know what you were doing.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Some people lived there. I don’t know what happened to them. They say they lost somebody at Rock Fence a long time ago – wonder what happened to them? They moved to Ross Mountain and they have a lot of pigs up there. They used to say they would throw you in there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: If they do something to you, they’ll throw you in with the pigs and they’ll eat you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they believe it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, some people believe it. That’s why they were scared to go there. People who lived up there didn’t think nothing about it.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: We didn’t know anything. Just to feed pigs.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just feeding them corn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Word was out that y’all were dangerous, and y’all didn’t know anything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Does Charlie still live there?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah. He was really eating when I went to see him a while back. It’s been a long time since I’ve seen him, and we just live close by. He was just going like this [gestures] chewing bread.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can just see him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did he feed you?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: No, they didn’t say anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They didn’t say, “Let’s eat?”

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: He might’ve said, “Go sit outside and when I get through eating, we’ll talk.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some people will say that to you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, some people will say that to you.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’ve been there before. We would never say that to anybody, huh. I’ve been somewhere where I was told that. I was thinking to myself, I was hungry.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: My stomach was growling.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was he eating beans or what?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I thought maybe... His hands – the way he was doing – I was thinking he had his hands like a raccoon. He was chewing. That’s how it is when I’m somewhere. No matter where, we’ll just talk for a little while. After a while, just like that, you’ll all be laughing when I’m talking about things. If it gets really serious sometimes, it’ll just break up. I’m gonna say it in English, you gotta put a little humor in it and it’ll get better.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just like when Charlie was eating.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Just like a raccoon. He would roll it around just like a raccoon does.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just like he was playing music. I bet he really made a sound when he was chewing it.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: If you weren’t hard of hearing, you could hear what he was doing. [chump chump] he was saying. It was like that there, especially when he lived there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was really funny. If you knew that one he’s talking about [talking to Guy] He hasn’t came here has he? Do think he would do?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: I don’t know. It’s pretty hard with him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some of them pretty bashful, huh?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: It’s because they don’t have good education. That’s what holds them back. They’re bashful to say something because they think, “I’ll say something wrong.” You couldn’t say it different, it’s in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s the way we like it here, we’re all speaking in Cherokee. Even if it’s for an hour.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: You could sat around all night with me. My visitors would play dominoes looking like this [gestures] sitting there looking at me listening. I would tell them, “Someone else talk!”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who all would be there? I’m not being nosey.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Just my friends. Sometimes Rick Duncan or them Glass boys. There’s this Mexican friend of mine. Sometimes he would come and see me and if I need to give the horses water, he would give them water and he would feed them and everything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s doing good for you.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: And he would say, “OK amigo, I going home,” and he would go home.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Are you talking about Roger, them Glass boys?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Really just Daks. The youngest.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I haven’t seen him in a long time.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: When I used to drive a truck, I used to hire him to feed the horses.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How many horses do you have?

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Boy, I just have four now. I used to have [unclear]..When I got sick, I started selling them, because I trained horses all my life. I’ve trained a lot of horses.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It really cost a lot to feed horses. I got pigs now and I’m finding out how expensive.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Now they’re gonna be afraid to go to your house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They’re gonna throw you in the pig pen.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There ain’t nobody comes to my house.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Do you still live way over there?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No, I live here in Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Oh, do you live over there by the railroad track? Or, I mean, over by the water?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, at Welling where we used to milk cows. When my husband had the stroke, we moved from there and our youngest son lives there, and we bought another place with two acres because we couldn’t take care of that place. And now our boy lives there. We moved just a little down the way from there. We milked cows for about 30 years. I think about that, “How did I do it?”

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: You really wouldn’t think you could have done it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But if you had to do it you would do it without thinking about it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, what do you think, how much do we lack?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Six minutes. Is there anything else you wanna talk about? You told some funny things.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Y’all might tell on me if I did.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You told some funny things.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Not really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you talked about those Glasses, there’s some close by from where I’m from. Long Prairie. The Glass family.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Yeah, I know them, too. I’m really not that old, but there is a lot of people who know me and I know them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really just here the other day they lost a Glass boy. He disappeared for about two or three months. And they found him laying in a well.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did he just fall?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They don’t know what happened.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Well, somebody don’t just fall in.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they say, but cops are still looking into it or at least that’s what they say, but I don’t know. Nowadays when something happens to a Cherokee, nobody pays attention to what happened.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There’s a song, are we gonna dance?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-uh

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: That’s me, a broken-down cowboy.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Are we finished now?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we’re done.

segments.speaker: richard-ross
segments.translation: Let’s all just go home. Here’s that horse I had – I sold it for a thousand dollars.
